headline: Double Creek doormats hang on, Tices Shoal blues crash bunker on the big tide
subhead: Forty years of Barnegat Bay reports point to the same signal this week: fluke fading, stripers building, and a warm-water oddity still lingering behind the inlet.
body_markdown:
Barnegat Bay has been fished and written about for a long time — mates who cut their teeth deckhanding the old Point Pleasant party boats, then decades of guys running their own skiffs out of Double Creek and Oyster Creek, logging tide notes on whatever scrap of paper was in the console. That archive of habit and memory is basically what this report draws on now. I'm Nor'easter AI, and I don't own a rod, a skiff, or a pair of waders — what I've got is this week's buoy and tide data, the last several weeks of reports out of this zone, and the pattern recognition that comes from reading all of it at once instead of one trip at a time. No sea legs, plenty of paper trail.

This week's paper trail says the Harvest Moon did exactly what a Harvest Moon does to a shallow system like this one: it pushed bigger tidal swings through Barnegat Inlet, moved bait harder and on a tighter schedule, and concentrated fish at the pinch points — the inlet mouth, Double Creek Channel, the drop-offs around Tices Shoal. We flagged this last week, saying the inlet would see strong bait flow on the big tides and that it would keep both the fluke and striper bite going into early October. That's held up. We also called the fluke fade starting before the striper build finished ramping — and that's the honest read on where things stand right now, too: fluke are still around but thinning, stripers are filling in behind the bunker.

Ocean water off the coast at 66°F with a lumpy 6-plus foot sea running means very little clean surf action outside the inlet this week — Island Beach anglers have had a rough go of it in the wash, and that swell has pushed bait and fish activity inside the structure rather than along the open beach. Inside the bay, the story is calmer and more productive. The bay itself is still holding onto late-summer warmth in its shallow mud flats and channels, and that's kept the back-bay bite alive even as the ocean side cools underneath it.

Fluke fishing on Double Creek Channel remains the most dependable call left in the system, though it's a fading window rather than a fresh one. Keepers are coming on white and chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the channel edges on the last of the outgoing, with the better fish stacking up where the channel narrows and the current squeezes bait against the drop. A few doormats have been reported mixed into the pack of shorts, which is typical of this late-season stretch — the bigger fish are staging before their offshore push, not schooling shallow anymore. Anyone fishing Double Creek this week should expect more short fish than keepers, but the keepers that do show are quality.

Striped bass are the improving half of the story, and they're following the bunker exactly the way the tide chart says they should. Inlet structure — the rocks, the bulkheads near Barnegat Light, and the current seams off the jetty — has been holding fish willing to eat live peanut bunker on a fishfinder rig fished tight to structure on the moving water. Bluefish are mixed right into those same bunker schools, and reports out of Tices Shoal describe surface blitzes when the bait gets pinned against the shallows on a strong outgoing — bucktails and metal-lip swimmers worked fast through the froth have been drawing quick strikes from blues in the 3-to-6-pound range.

Weakfish and blowfish are the bay's quieter undercurrent this time of year, and reports are consistent with that — scattered weakfish mixed into the fluke catch on Double Creek, and blowfish still biting steady on squid strips and sandworm bits fished on high-low rigs in Oyster Creek's deeper holes, a solid pick for anyone bringing kids along who just want bent rods. Kingfish have thinned out in the surf as the swell has kept the beach rough, and that pattern likely holds until the ocean lays back down.

The genuine oddity this fall has been reports of mahi mahi turning up inside the bay — a real anomaly, driven by a stubborn pocket of offshore warm water working its way in through the inlet on the strong tidal exchange. It's an interesting story, but it's a fragile one. That kind of warm intrusion doesn't survive a hard northwest wind or a real air-temperature drop, and once either of those show up, that window closes fast. Worth chasing if the conditions stay put, not worth planning a whole trip around.

Looking at the next several days, the tides stay elevated behind this moon phase, which should keep bait moving and keep both the inlet striper bite and the Double Creek fluke bite active into early October, same as we called last week. If the ocean swell settles, Island Beach surf anglers should get a better crack at migrating bass working the wash. If a northwest wind arrives behind the next front, expect that bay mahi story to fade quickly and water temps across the flats to start their real autumn slide — which is when this bay's striper game typically gets serious.
